title: A photo from phone to phone
description: A photo becomes binary numbers at the camera sensor, is handled by transistor switches following software, crosses the internet as packets and is rebuilt as pixels.

facts.text: A digital camera's sensor is covered in light receptors, or pixels; light striking them induces an electric current that is translated into binary digits for storage.
During each clock cycle, billions of transistors, tiny switches, open and close inside a processor.
Software is the programs, the instructions that tell a computer's hardware what to do.
The internet is a network of networks: routers link local networks, and internet service providers link their routers to each other.
Packet switching breaks data into small packets that travel independently over any available route and are reassembled at the destination.
On a screen, an image is a grid of pixels, each a mix of red, green and blue light set by numbers.

title: What a bit is
description: A bit, short for binary digit, holds one choice between two alternatives, 1 or 0; in hardware a transistor on or off stores it. Tukey coined the word (1947); Shannon first printed it (1948).

facts.text: A bit, short for binary digit, is the unit of information given by one choice between two alternatives, written 1 or 0.
In a computer, a transistor switch stores a bit: on is 1 and off is 0.
John Tukey is credited with first using the word bit, a blend of binary and digit, for a unit of information, in a 1947 memo.
Claude Shannon's 1948 paper contains the first published use of the word bit.

title: Each bit doubles the patterns
description: Every added bit doubles the number of patterns: 1 bit 2, 2 bits 4, 3 bits 8, so a byte of 8 bits has 256.

facts.text: 1 bit gives 2 patterns (0, 1); 2 bits give 4 (00, 01, 10, 11); 3 bits give 8: each added bit doubles the number of patterns.
A byte is 8 bits, which can make 256 different patterns: doubling from 2 eight times gives 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256.

title: Kilo, mega, giga, tera
description: Storage sizes count bytes with the metric prefixes: kilo, mega, giga and tera mean a thousand, a million, a billion and a trillion, each step 1,000 times the last.

facts.text: Kilo, mega, giga and tera mean a thousand, a million, a billion and a trillion: each step up is 1,000 times the last.
One byte is enough to hold about one typed character, so a few dozen characters of plain text take a few dozen bytes.

title: How big a photo, a movie and a drive are
description: A 24.2-megapixel photo is about 73 MB raw and about 3.6 MB as JPEG; HD streaming uses up to 3 GB an hour; a 1 TB drive holds a trillion bytes.

facts.text: A 24.2-megapixel camera takes photos of 6,016 by 4,016 pixels, about 24 million pixels.
Stored at 3 bytes per pixel (one each for red, green and blue), a 24.2-megapixel photo takes about 72.6 million bytes, about 73 MB.
JPEG compression of 20 to 1 is easily done with practically invisible loss of quality, which would shrink a 73 MB photo to about 3.6 MB.
Netflix says streaming in high definition uses up to 3 GB per hour, so a two-hour film uses up to 6 GB.

title: Why a 1 TB drive shows 931 GB
description: Drive makers count a terabyte as 10^12 bytes; Windows counts a gigabyte as 1,073,741,824 bytes (1,024 cubed), so a 1 TB drive shows about 931 GB. No bytes are missing.

facts.text: A 1 TB drive holds 1,000,000,000,000 bytes; Windows counts a gigabyte as 1,073,741,824 bytes (1,024 × 1,024 × 1,024), so it shows the drive as about 931 GB.

title: ASCII: letters as numbers
description: ASCII (1963) gives letters, digits and punctuation standard numbers using 7 bits, so 128 characters; A is 65, and upper and lower case differ by one bit.

facts.text: ASCII, approved as an American standard in 1963, uses 7-bit binary numbers, so it can represent 128 different characters.
In ASCII, uppercase A is the number 65 and B is 66.
In ASCII, 1010000 is uppercase P and 1110000 is lowercase p: the two codes differ in a single bit.

title: Unicode and emoji
description: Unicode gives every character in every writing system a unique number, replacing hundreds of clashing encodings; emoji are Unicode numbers that each phone maker draws its own way.

facts.text: Before Unicode there were hundreds of character encodings, and they conflicted: two could use the same number for two different characters.
Unicode gives a unique number to every character, whatever the platform, program or language.
Unicode 18.0, released in September 2026, holds 172,808 characters.
UTF-8, a form of Unicode, is backward-compatible with ASCII: ASCII's numbers still work.
The Unicode Consortium standardizes emoji codes; a phone receives an emoji as a number and draws it, so its style can differ between device makers.

title: Pixels as three numbers
description: A digital image is a grid of pixels; each pixel mixes red, green and blue light, each a number from 0 to 255 (one byte), giving 16,777,216 possible colors.

facts.text: A digital image is a grid of pixels, each a small square of one color.
Each pixel's color is a mix of red, green and blue light, each set by a number from 0 (off) to 255 (full brightness), which fits in one byte.
Three values of 0 to 255 give 256 × 256 × 256 = 16,777,216 possible colors.

title: Sound as samples
description: Digital audio measures the sound wave at equal time intervals and stores each sample as a binary number; CDs take 44,100 samples a second, more than twice the top of human hearing.

facts.text: Digital recording samples the sound wave at points spaced at equal time intervals and encodes each sampled point as a binary number.
CDs sample sound 44,100 times a second (44.1 kHz).
Sampling must happen more than twice as fast as the highest frequency to capture; hearing reaches about 20 kHz, so CD audio needed more than about 40 kHz, 40,000 samples a second.

title: AND, OR and NOT gates
description: A logic gate turns yes-or-no inputs into one yes-or-no output: AND needs all inputs 1, OR needs any, NOT flips its input. Gates are built from transistors.

facts.text: A logic gate takes yes-or-no inputs (1 or 0) and produces one output, working like a switch that passes or blocks electrical pulses.
An AND gate outputs 1 only when all its inputs are 1; an OR gate outputs 1 if any input is 1.
A NOT gate, or inverter, outputs the opposite of its input: 1 becomes 0 and 0 becomes 1.
Logic gate circuits are built from components such as transistors.
A lamp with two switches in series lights only when both are closed (AND); with two switches in parallel it lights when either is closed (OR).
Connected together, logic gates can carry out arithmetic.

title: Boolean algebra meets switches
description: Boole (1847, 1854) built an algebra of true and false, 1 and 0; Shannon's master's thesis used it to lay the theory of switching circuits, the basis of digital circuits.

facts.text: George Boole began the algebra of logic, now called Boolean algebra, in 1847 and 1854; it treats statements as true or false, written 1 and 0.
Claude Shannon's master's thesis, A Symbolic Analysis of Relay and Switching Circuits, used Boolean algebra to lay the theoretical groundwork of digital circuits.

title: Adding in binary
description: Binary sums have four cases: 0+0=0, 0+1=1, 1+0=1 and 1+1=10, where a 1 is carried to the next place, just as in decimal.

facts.text: Adding two bits has four cases: 0 + 0 = 0, 0 + 1 = 1, 1 + 0 = 1, and 1 + 1 = 10, a 0 with a 1 carried to the next place.
In binary, 3 + 1 is 11 + 01: the carries ripple left twice and give 100, which is 4.

title: Half and full adders
description: A half adder is an exclusive-OR (sum) plus an AND (carry); a full adder also takes the carry in, and full adders chained carry to carry add numbers of any length.

facts.text: A half adder adds two bits: its sum is exclusive OR, 1 when exactly one input is 1, and its carry is AND, 1 only when both are 1.
A half adder's sum, (A AND NOT B) OR (NOT A AND B), is built from AND, OR and NOT gates.
A full adder adds three bits, two digits plus the carry from the place to its right; full adders chained, each carry feeding the next, add longer binary numbers.
A processor's arithmetic-logic unit does addition, subtraction, multiplication and division, plus logic operations such as comparing data.

title: The fetch, decode, execute cycle
description: The processor fetches the instruction at the program counter's address, decodes its binary pattern, executes it, then repeats; jumps change the counter.

facts.text: A processor fetches the instruction at the address in its program counter, decodes the instruction's binary pattern into fields with meanings, and executes the operation.
After a fetch, the program counter usually steps on to the next instruction; jumps and branches can change it to point somewhere else.
When one instruction is executed, the cycle begins again with the next.

title: The clock and gigahertz
description: A clock sends pulses at a fixed rate to regulate the cycle; gigahertz counts billions of cycles a second, so 3.2 GHz is 3.2 billion.

facts.text: A clock emitting pulses at a fixed, precise frequency regulates the fetch, decode and execute cycle.
Clock speed counts the cycles a processor runs per second in gigahertz: a 3.2 GHz processor runs 3.2 billion cycles a second.

title: Memory in layers
description: Memory runs from fast, expensive registers and SRAM cache on the CPU to denser, slower DRAM main memory and slower, cheaper nonvolatile storage, because main memory lags the CPU.

facts.text: DRAM main memory typically takes 20 to 80 nanoseconds to access data, while a processor arithmetic operation may take a nanosecond or less.
Memory is organized as a hierarchy, from fast, expensive registers in the processor to slower, cheaper nonvolatile storage.
A processor has a small number of registers, very fast memory holding the current instructions and the data they work on.
Cache is fast SRAM on the processor chip, up to several megabytes, holding frequently used instructions and data.
SRAM is fast but physically large; a chip the same size holds several times as much DRAM, which is slower.
Main memory made of DRAM loses its contents when the power is turned off; storage is nonvolatile and keeps them.

title: Why a small cache works
description: Programs repeat instructions in loops and use related data (locality of reference), so after values are copied into cache, many requests are served from it.

facts.text: Programs show locality of reference, repeating the same instructions in loops and using related data, so once values are copied into cache, requests can be served from it.

title: Same bits, different meanings
description: Bits carry no meaning by themselves: the bytes 72, 73, 33 spell HI! as text or make a shade of yellow as a color. Context, such as the file format, decides.

facts.text: The bytes 72, 73 and 33 spell HI! when read as ASCII text, and are a shade of yellow when read as red, green and blue; as plain numbers they sum to 178.
Context, such as the file format, decides whether a program reads the same bits as numbers, text or colors.
